Instructions to candidates: Answer any FOUR questions. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Discuss three topographic features of the sea floor.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The floor of the oceans is not flat: it has a varied relief which is a result of plate tectonics, sedimentation and volcanism. Three major features, from the continent outwards (and drawn in a simple cross-section of an ocean from coast to centre), are discussed below.

**1. The continental shelf (with its slope).** This is the **gently sloping (about $0.1^\circ$), shallow platform** which is the **submerged edge of the continent**, between the coast and the **shelf break**, at a depth of about 130 to 200 m. It is from a few kilometres to several hundred kilometres wide (wide on passive margins, narrow on active margins). It is covered by sediments from the land (sands, muds) and by shelly and coral limestones, and it is the **richest area for fish, oil, gas and sand**. Beyond the shelf break the **continental slope** descends steeply (several degrees) to the deep ocean floor, and it is cut by **submarine canyons** through which turbidity currents carry sediment to the **continental rise** and the deep sea fan.

**2. The mid-ocean ridge.** The **mid-ocean ridge** is a **continuous submarine mountain chain** (about 65 000 km long) which rises about 2 to 3 km above the deep floor and has a **central rift valley** along its crest. It is the **diverging plate boundary** where **new basaltic oceanic crust is formed by sea-floor spreading**; it is offset by **transform faults** and is the site of **shallow earthquakes, volcanoes and hydrothermal vents (black smokers)**. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the best known example. On both sides, the crust becomes older and the ridge subsides, and the sediment cover thickens with distance.

**3. The ocean trench.** A trench is a **long, narrow, very deep (up to about 11 km) and steep-sided depression**, which marks a **convergent (subduction) plate boundary**, where the dense oceanic plate bends down into the mantle. It is the **deepest part of the ocean**, is associated with **deep and shallow earthquakes (the Benioff zone) and a volcanic island arc or mountain chain** on the overriding plate, and collects sediment from the land and ocean (accretionary wedge). The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is the deepest.

*Other features which could be discussed instead:* the **abyssal plain** (very flat plain at 4 to 6 km depth covered by fine sediment), **seamounts and guyots** (submarine volcanoes, flat-topped when eroded at sea level) and **volcanic island chains** above hot spots.
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Define an intrusion.

(2 marks)

(ii) Describe four major intrusive igneous bodies.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Intrusion.** An intrusion is a **body of igneous rock that is formed when magma is forced into (and cools and crystallises within) the pre-existing country rock below the surface**, without reaching the surface. It is younger than the rock it invades and produces **coarse- to medium-grained (plutonic or hypabyssal) rocks**; the country rock next to it may show a **contact (thermal) aureole**.

**(ii) Four major intrusive bodies.** They are classified by their **shape and by their relationship to the bedding of the country rock**: **concordant** (parallel to the layers) or **discordant** (cutting across them).

1. **Batholith** (discordant). The **largest intrusion**, with an outcrop of more than 100 square kilometres, an **irregular, dome-shaped mass** with **steep sides which widen downwards and have no visible floor**. It is composed of **coarse-grained granite or granodiorite** and is formed in the cores of **fold mountain belts** by the slow cooling of huge quantities of magma at depth. It is exposed only after deep erosion. Example: the Sierra Nevada batholith (California).
2. **Sill** (concordant). A **tabular (sheet-like) body, parallel to the bedding of the sedimentary country rock**, usually **horizontal or gently dipping**, which has **baked contacts above and below** and is of **medium-grained basic rock (dolerite)**, often with columnar joints at right angles to the walls. Example: the Whin Sill (England).
3. **Dyke** (discordant). A **vertical or steeply inclined sheet-like body** which **cuts across the bedding** (and across older structures), a few centimetres to many metres wide and long, with **chilled margins** and **baked country rock**, and usually made of dolerite or basalt. Dykes occur singly, in parallel **swarms** or in radial patterns around volcanoes, and they fill fractures.
4. **Laccolith** (concordant). A **lens-shaped or mushroom-shaped body with a flat floor and a domed roof**, which **forces the overlying strata upwards into a dome** because the magma is viscous (intermediate or acid) and does not spread far. It is fed from below by a feeder dyke. Example: the Henry Mountains (Utah).

*Other bodies (not needed):* stock or boss (small discordant plutons), lopolith (saucer-shaped), ring dyke, cone sheets and volcanic plug. A labelled **block diagram showing all of them in the same country rock** gives the best illustration.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Explain four magmatic differentiation processes in basaltic magma.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Magmatic differentiation** is the group of processes by which **one parent magma (here a basaltic magma) gives rise to igneous rocks of different composition**. Four processes are explained.

**1. Fractional crystallisation (with crystal settling).** As the basaltic magma cools, the minerals crystallise **in the order of Bowen's reaction series**: first the **high-temperature, dense, iron- and magnesium-rich** minerals (olivine, then pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase). If these crystals are **removed from the liquid** (they are denser than the magma and **sink under gravity** to form layers called cumulates at the floor of the chamber, or they are removed by filter pressing), they **cannot react with the liquid**. The **residual liquid becomes progressively richer in silica, sodium, potassium and water** and poorer in iron, magnesium and calcium, so that successive magmas **change from basaltic to andesitic, then to dacitic and rhyolitic (granitic)**. This is the main process; it produces **layered intrusions** (for example the Skaergaard intrusion in Greenland).

**2. Assimilation (contamination) of country rock.** The hot magma **melts or dissolves pieces of the wall rock (xenoliths) or reacts with them**, taking their chemical components into the magma, so that its composition is changed (for example a basalt which assimilates silica-rich crustal rock becomes more silica-rich). The heat needed is supplied by the **crystallisation of the magma itself**, so assimilation is limited and is usually combined with fractional crystallisation.

**3. Magma mixing.** Two magmas of **different composition** (for example a hot basaltic magma which is injected into a chamber of cooler, more silicic magma) **mix** in the chamber before solidification, giving **hybrid magmas** of intermediate composition (andesite). Evidence: **mixed (disequilibrium) mineral assemblages** and **mafic enclaves** in granites and andesites.

**4. Liquid immiscibility.** On cooling, a homogeneous magma may **separate into two liquids that do not mix**, like oil and water, for example **a dense iron-sulphide (or iron- and titanium-rich) liquid and a silicate liquid**. The dense droplets **sink and collect** at the base of the intrusion, which explains **massive nickel-copper sulphide and iron-titanium oxide ores**, and the **silicate-rich liquid** goes on to evolve separately.

*(Flow differentiation, in which crystals migrate to the centre of a flowing magma in a dyke or sill, and gas transfer are other processes which can replace any of these.)*
